verses.text: Now Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest, who was chief officer in Yahweh’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things.
Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, which was in Yahweh’s house.
On the next day, Pashhur released Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then Jeremiah said to him, “Yahweh has not called your name Pashhur, but Magormissabib.

For Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself, and to all your friends; and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and your eyes shall see it; and I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall carry them captive to Babylon, and shall kill them with the sword.

Moreover I will give all the riches of this city, and all its gains, and all the precious things of it, yes, all the treasures of the kings of Judah will I give into the hand of their enemies; and they shall make them captives, and take them, and carry them to Babylon.

You, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house shall go into captivity; and you shall come to Babylon, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you, and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely.’”
Yahweh, you have persuaded me, and I was persuaded; you are stronger than I, and have prevailed. I have become a laughing-stock all day. Every one mocks me.
For as often as I speak, I cry out; I cry, Violence and destruction! because Yahweh’s word has been made a reproach to me, and a derision, all day.
If I say, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I can’t.

For I have heard the defaming of many, “Terror on every side! Denounce, and we will denounce him!” say all my familiar friends, those who watch for my fall. “Perhaps he will be persuaded, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him.”

But Yahweh is with me as an awesome mighty one. Therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail. They shall be utterly disappointed, because they have not dealt wisely, even with an everlasting dishonor which shall never be forgotten.
But, Yahweh of Armies, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance on them; for to you I have revealed my cause.
Sing to Yahweh, praise Yahweh; for he has delivered the soul of the needy from the hand of evildoers.
Cursed is the day in which I was born. Don’t let the day in which my mother bore me be blessed.
Cursed is the man who brought news to my father, saying, “A boy is born to you,” making him very glad.
Let that man be as the cities which Yahweh overthrew, and didn’t repent. Let him hear a cry in the morning, and shouting at noontime;
because he didn’t kill me from the womb; and so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb always great.
Why did I come out of the womb to see labor and sorrow, that my days should be consumed with shame?

footnotes.content: Pashhur was chief officer in the temple—a man with rank and comfort. Yet he heard the prophet's words and his heart hardened rather than softened. I've seen this: those closest to the house of God can grow furthest from His truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A priest struck a prophet in the very house of God. The world will always strike the messengers of truth. But notice: Pashhur's blow could mark Jeremiah's body, never his calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When released, Jeremiah renamed him—"Magor-Missabib," terror on every side. The Lord Himself renamed him. This is not cruelty but clarity: we choose our names by our choices. Terror follows those who fight God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pashhur will become his own worst terror—an exile watching the ruin his resistance helped bring. The Lord speaks judgment not in hatred but as consequence. Our path away from Him always loops back to frighten us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the riches of the city—every treasure—becomes spoil. What we cling to in faithlessness becomes our shame. The Lord does not hide wealth in secret; He gives it freely to those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pashhur shall die in exile—in Babylon, far from home, buried among those he prophesied falsely with. The company of our choices outlasts us. This is why I've learned: speak truth early, when it costs less.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Jeremiah speaks his heart: the Lord persuaded him, and he was persuaded—yes, but at what cost? Mockery all day long. This is the honest prayer of a faithful servant. The Lord honors such honesty; He does not demand we pretend the cost is nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every word becomes reproach and derision. Jeremiah speaks of violence and destruction—the only message the Lord gave him to give. When truth is unwelcome, the one who speaks it bears the world's scorn. I have seen such men; they never speak for ease.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If I say I will not speak," Jeremiah confesses, "a burning fire is shut up in my bones." This is the righteous constraint: to stay silent would be to betray the God who called us. We cannot help but speak when we've tasted His word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Terror on every side!"—familiar friends become enemies, watching for his fall. In betrayal, we learn: the world's counsel is not counsel but conspiracy. Yet Jeremiah reports it all plainly. No embellishment. This was his trust: speak truth and let God defend it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh is with me as an awesome mighty one." Even in the storm of mockery, Jeremiah plants this anchor: the Lord is not far off but beside him—mighty. His persecutors will stumble; they have built on foolishness. This is the heart that endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah calls on the Lord who tests the righteous and sees the heart and mind. He asks to see vengeance on his foes. This is raw prayer—not polished, not gentle, but true. The Lord's ear is open to the tested servant's plea.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then suddenly—joy breaks through. "Sing to Yahweh, praise Yahweh; for he has delivered the soul of the needy from the hand of evildoers." The tested heart knows rescue. This is worship that has walked through fire and emerged praising.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Jeremiah turns and curses the day he was born. Joy gives way to despair—the honest servant's struggle. In a single breath he praises and questions. This teaches me that faith is not one note but a whole song, major and minor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He curses the man who brought news of his birth to his father. In his pain, Jeremiah wishes he had never been born at all. Such words come only when the cost is truly high. The Lord does not reject the prophet for this prayer; He hears the depth of the trial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let that man be as the cities which Yahweh overthrew." Jeremiah invokes Sodom and Gomorrah—utter destruction. This is the speech of a man pressed beyond measure, yet even here he appeals to God's justice, not his own vengeance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He didn't kill me from the womb." In his darkest moment, Jeremiah wishes he had never drawn breath. How low a faithful servant can fall—and how the Lord still holds him, still uses him, even in this despair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in these final words: many of us have asked, "Why was I born to see such sorrow?" In our trials, we stand with Jeremiah—not alone in our questioning, but held by the same God who held him. Our lament is heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
